FEATHER vs FEATHER_new — tiny synthetic A–E graph, by-hand math check

No OSM / Overpass, no cached city graph, no amenity lookup — just a hand-built 5-node graph so every matrix and embedding value can be checked against pen-and-paper math. Graph (edge: length):
  • A-B: 1
  • B-E: 3
  • E-D: 3
  • A-C: 2
  • C-D: 1
  • A-D: 5
D is treated as the "amenity" / destination node.

Build the synthetic graph

Nodes are relabeled 0..n-1 (FEATHER / FEATHER_new both expect nx.adjacency_matrix(graph, nodelist=range(n))), but every table below is shown with the original A–E letters as row/column labels so it stays easy to read.

Feature vector X

D is the amenity / end node — a natural, easy-to-hand-check feature is each node's shortest-path distance to D (weighted by length). Swap this out for whatever feature you're actually verifying.
FEATHER (unweighted — every edge counts equally, length ignored)

FEATHER_new (weighted, w = 1/length)

A quirk worth knowing about: FEATHER_new._create_D_inverse reads the edge attribute literally named "weight". Our graph only carries "length", so calling _create_D_inverse(graph) directly on the raw graph silently falls back to unweighted degree (every edge counts as 1) instead of summing 1/length. _create_A_tilde avoids this internally by building a local copy with weight = 1/length set before calling _create_D_inverse on it — so A_tilde_w itself is correct, but a standalone D_inverse_w printed from the raw graph would not match it. To show the D_inverse_w that is actually consistent with A_tilde_w (and with hand math), we replicate that same weight = 1/length assignment below before calling _create_D_inverse.

Visualizing FEATHER_new across theta

This reproduces the chart your partner built in Excel: x-axis is the characteristic function evaluation point (theta), y-axis is the embedding value at that point. Each node gets its own curve set — one line per (scale, real/imaginary) combination — plus one more chart for the unweighted average across all five nodes. Blue = real part, orange = imaginary part. Line style marks the random-walk scale: solid = scale 1, dashed = scale 2, dotted = scale 3, and so on if you push order higher with the sliders above.

Average chart, styled after Figure 1 of the FEATHER paper

This redoes just the "Average across nodes" chart to look like the paper's Figure 1 — "the real part of ... mean characteristic functions with standard deviations around the mean": one line per scale (the real-part mean across the 5 nodes) with a shaded ± 1 standard deviation band around it, boxed axes, dashed gridlines, and a bordered legend underneath the plot. The per-node panels above keep their original look — only this chart is restyled. The curve itself is not just the 5 stored evaluation points joined by straight lines. θ is a continuous real-valued input to cos/sin, so the characteristic function is a genuine smooth wave — we re-evaluate the same scale-r random-walk weighted formula (A_tilde^r · cos(x ⊗ θ)) at hundreds of closely spaced θ values to draw the actual curve, then mark the handful of θ values that are actually stored in the embedding / Excel file as dots sitting right on top of it.
